nodes.statement: An experience is identical to the cause–effect structure (Φ-structure) unfolded from a maximal substrate; quality and quantity of experience are completely specified by the MICS and Φ value.
Consciousness requires intrinsic, integrated, irreducible cause–effect power within the substrate itself, independent of any external observer.
A feed-forward system functionally equivalent to a conscious complex is not conscious, because functional equivalence without intrinsic integrated information is insufficient for experience.

The physical correlate of consciousness is the Φ-structure specified by the substrate in its current state, not the substrate per se; minor state changes can cause major changes in the Φ-structure and thus in experience.

Every property of an experience is identical to a property of the cause–effect structure specified by a substrate satisfying IIT's postulates; the identity is between intrinsic (subjective) and extrinsic (objective) existence, not between two substances.
The maximally irreducible conceptual structure (MICS) generated by a complex is identical to its experience; its quantity is specified by Φ-max (integrated information).
Only mechanisms that specify integrated information—information generated by the whole above and beyond its parts, making it irreducible—can contribute to consciousness.
The exclusion postulate restricts the locus of consciousness to a single maximally irreducible system (complex), not any subset or superset.

The quality of experience corresponds to the Φ-structure (cause–effect structure of distinctions and relations), and the quantity of experience corresponds to Φ, the sum of integrated information of distinctions and relations.
Existence and consciousness must be evaluated from the intrinsic perspective of the entity itself, not from the perspective of an external observer.
Experience is unified and irreducible to non-interdependent components; integration is an axiomatic property of every experience.
Mechanisms that do not generate integrated information do not exist from the intrinsic perspective of a system; integrated information is the threshold condition for causal/experiential existence.
The richness and level of consciousness increase with the diversity and specialization of causal connections; homogeneous connectivity reduces consciousness.
Digital computers running von Neumann architectures are not conscious even if they simulate cognition; the architecture of the substrate determines consciousness.
The physical substrate of consciousness has a definite spatial grain, timescale, and state-space determined by maxima of cause–effect power, identifiable empirically via perturbation and observation.

High Φmax (and thus consciousness) requires convergent-divergent integration; feedforward, modular architectures like the cerebellum cannot form a large complex and are excluded from the conscious substrate.

The PSC is a bounded complex of elements with maximal integrated information; elements outside this boundary (e.g., cerebellar neurons, peripheral sensory/motor pathways, basal ganglia loops) do not directly contribute to consciousness despite influencing cortical activity.
Conscious information is not transmitted or broadcast from one brain region to another; the locus of consciousness is intrinsic to the PSC, not a relay or global broadcast.
Consciousness fades when bistability causes breakdown of information integration despite ongoing neural activity, establishing a functional threshold for consciousness tied to integration capacity.

Consciousness corresponds to integrated information (Φ) that is irreducible to that specified by a system's parts; the quality of experience maps to the form of the conceptual structure specified by the PSC.

The PSC operates at a definite spatio-temporal grain (local cortical neuron groups over ~100 ms intervals); perturbations at the appropriate grain change experience, fixing the mechanism scale of consciousness.

IIT predicts that loss and recovery of consciousness is associated with breakdown and recovery of information integration capacity, measurable via the perturbational complexity index (PCI) derived from TMS-EEG responses.

IIT predicts that the neural substrate of consciousness (PSC/complex) corresponds to elements with maximum intrinsic cause–effect power, locating the content-specific NCC in the neural elements of the PSC rather than in prefrontal or other regions, consistent with a posterior cortical hot zone.

IIT predicts that the duration of a conscious instant is definite and sustained over tens to hundreds of milliseconds, not transient or phasic, as required by the exclusion postulate governing the cause–effect structure of the PSC.
Conscious moments arise from objective reduction (OR) of quantum superpositions at a threshold defined by τ ≈ ℏ/EG in spacetime geometry.
Conscious events are terminations of quantum computations in brain microtubules; consciousness is substrate-dependent on specific biological structures.
The quantum state reduction (OR) is a non-computable physical process outside standard unitary quantum formalism, making conscious moments non-computable.
Proto-conscious experience is an intrinsic feature of every OR event throughout the universe, not confined to brains; consciousness is fundamental to physical law.
OR is a real, objective physical phenomenon independent of any observer, not an approximation or shift in observer viewpoint.

Orch OR events occur specifically inside neuronal dendrites and soma (microtubules), locating the mechanism of consciousness at the subcellular quantum level rather than at the level of neuronal network computation.
Conscious moments correlate with orchestrated OR events reaching the gravitational threshold on timescales of 10 to several hundred milliseconds, tying consciousness to a specific temporal profile.

Consciousness is not merely an observer that collapses the wavefunction (Copenhagen) nor a splitting stream across parallel worlds; it is identified with objective physical reduction events in quantum systems.

Conscious moments arise from Orchestrated Objective Reduction (Orch OR) of quantum superpositions in microtubules, where the reduction time τ ≈ ℏ/EG determines the timing and intensity of each conscious moment.
Consciousness is not an emergent property of complex neuronal computation but is rooted in primitive experiential qualities inherent in OR events occurring throughout the universe.
Conscious experience is temporally non-local to a degree determined by the Orch OR process timescale, meaning internal conscious timing need not align with external clock progression.

bridge.note: Decidable ONLY IF microtubule quantum states measurably modulate network-scale integration (e.g. under anesthesia).
